passages.where: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, and his examples are light and darkness, Christ and Belial, the temple of God and idols. The site's plain note says most readers think his first concern was sharing in idol worship and any tie that would draw believers back into it, and that Christians answer differently how far the command reaches beyond that. All agree on its heart: a believer should not enter a bond that requires splitting loyalty to Christ.

Paul tells a widow that she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord. The site's note on 2 Corinthians 6 calls this the more direct statement of the principle many churches teach for marriage. Paul gives freedom and a boundary in the same sentence.

When Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and he was not wholly devoted to the LORD as David had been. The site's note says the text does not treat wisdom as a guarantee of faithfulness: his heart turned gradually, through his loves. Understanding what is right and loving it with the whole heart are different things.

Ruth, a widow from Moab, refuses to leave her mother-in-law and pledges herself to Naomi's people, Naomi's God and Naomi's grave. The site's note says the book shows a Moabite woman embraced by Israel's God and people, who became the great-grandmother of David. Her faith was her own, given to Naomi's God before Boaz appears in the story, and Scripture's concern about marriage across faith is never contempt for another people.

To a believer already married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay, Paul says do not seek a divorce, for the unbelieving spouse and the children are made holy through the believer. The site's plain note on 2 Corinthians 6 says no one should take the warning against being unequally yoked as a reason to leave a willing spouse, and that nothing here asks anyone to stay in danger. The passage ends with Paul's sober question to the believer whose spouse leaves: how do you know whether you will save them?

The Song's great statement is that love is as strong as death and that mighty waters cannot quench it. The site's note says the book teaches the goodness and power of love between a man and a woman within faithful commitment. That strength is why this question is so tender: by the time it is asked, the heart has usually moved already.

Jesus asks who would begin to build a tower without first sitting down to count the cost, and the site's note says the parable warns against a casual following that has not reckoned with the cross. He wants no one to follow him without knowing what it may cost. The same honesty belongs before any lifelong promise, especially one in which the deepest thing in your life cannot be shared.

Peter tells believers to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts and to be ready to give the reason for their hope to anyone who asks, with gentleness and respect. The site's note on the chapter speaks of explaining that hope with gentleness. A person who does not share your faith is owed honesty about what it means to you, and never contempt.

The father urges his son to trust the LORD with all his heart and not to lean on his own understanding. The site's note says the chapter's promises are proverbs about how life generally goes under God, not contracts. Trusting God here may mean believing that his way is good even when it costs you something you love.

David calls the LORD his chosen portion and his cup, the one who has made his lot secure. The site's note says the language comes from the division of the land and from the priests' privilege of having God, not land, as their share, and the plain note adds that this does not make every other good thing worthless. Whatever this decision costs, the psalm insists that the one who has the LORD has not been left with nothing.

misread.taken: Do not be unequally yoked is sometimes taken to mean that a believer should leave a husband or wife who does not believe, or should keep away from people who do not share the faith, or may look down on them.
misread.says: The site's plain note answers no to both. Paul himself tells a believer married to a willing unbeliever not to seek a divorce (1 Corinthians 7:12-13), and he had already told the Corinthians that keeping away from every sinner in the city was not what he meant, since they would have to leave the world. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. The note says believers are to be friends, neighbors, coworkers and good citizens with people of every faith and none, and that nothing here gives anyone a reason to look down on unbelievers.

misread.taken: Can two walk together without agreeing where to go is often quoted as a rule for dating and marriage, as if this verse were written about whom to marry.
misread.says: In Amos it is the first of a chain of questions about cause and effect, a lion that roars because it has prey, a trap that springs because something touched it, and the site's note says the chain leads to one conclusion: when the LORD has spoken, the prophet must speak. Amos is explaining why Israel's coming disaster is the LORD's doing and why he cannot keep quiet about it. The common sense of the question is true enough, but for marriage Scripture speaks more directly elsewhere, in Paul's word that a widow may marry one who belongs to the Lord.

whole: This is one of the tender questions, because the heart has usually moved before the question is asked. The person you care about may be kinder and more honest than some Christians you know. Friends may say it makes no difference, a parent may be quietly worried, and you may be hoping that in time they will come to share your faith. You may feel judged by your church for even asking, or you may already be married to someone who does not believe and wondering what this means for you. If the relationship has become controlling, or you are afraid, your safety comes first: tell someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The Bible's caution here is not contempt for people outside the faith. Ruth came from Moab and became the great-grandmother of David, and Peter tells believers to speak to everyone with gentleness and respect. The concern is the heart, and where it is turned. Solomon's loves turned his heart gradually, and he was the wisest man in Israel. Marriage joins two lives at the root, and for a Christian the root is Christ; to marry someone who does not share that is to promise your whole life to a person with whom the deepest thing in it cannot be shared. The temptations run both ways. It is easy to believe what we want to believe, to date someone as a project and to hope a person will change because we need them to. It is also easy for Christians to treat unbelievers as lesser, or as targets, which Scripture forbids.

So the Bible's wisdom is to count the cost honestly, and early. Ask what your faith actually is to you; if Christ is the center, ask what it would mean to build a home where the center cannot be shared, to raise children, to pray, to face death. Do not date anyone as a mission; Paul's question still stands, that no one can know whether they will save another. Be honest with the person you care about, gently and soon, about what your faith means and why it matters to how you choose. Talk with mature believers who know you, and listen if they are worried. If you decide to end a relationship for Christ's sake, it may be one of the hardest acts of faithfulness you ever do, and it is no judgment on the other person's worth. If you are already married to someone who does not believe, Paul's word is to stay if they are willing, to live in peace and to love them well, and it never asks you to stay in danger.

The hope beneath this is that God's love for the person you care about is greater than yours, and his purposes for them are not in your hands. Love is as strong as death, the Song says; Christ's love proved stronger than death, and it is the love that gives every other love its right place. Whatever this decision costs, the LORD is the portion of those who trust him, and they have not been left with nothing. Putting him first does not make your other loves smaller. It makes them truer.

differ.share: Christians agree that believers should be friends, neighbors and coworkers with people of every faith and none, that no one should leave a willing spouse because the spouse does not believe, that every person outside the faith bears God's image and is owed gentleness and respect, and that a believer should not enter a bond that requires splitting loyalty to Christ.

views.name: The verse speaks to marriage
views.body: Many churches teach from 2 Corinthians 6:14, set beside Paul's word that a widow may marry as long as her husband belongs to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39), that a believer should marry only a believer, and some apply the verse also to business partnerships and to joining bodies whose aims conflict with Christ.

views.name: The verse keeps close to its first setting
views.body: Others hold that Paul's first concern in 2 Corinthians 6 was sharing in idol worship and any tie that would draw believers back into it, and warn against making the verse a rule for every friendship or business dealing.

differ.after: The site's notes on 2 Corinthians 6 set out these readings and do not choose. Neither reading gives anyone a reason to leave a willing spouse or to look down on unbelievers.

sit: If Christ is the center of your life, what would it mean to share a home with someone who cannot share the center, and what would it cost you to be honest about that now?

prayer.lead: Asaph's confession that God is the strength of his heart and his portion forever. Pray it when a decision may cost you something you love.

careLines.text: Nothing here, or in 1 Corinthians 7, asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger
Nothing here gives anyone a reason to look down on unbelievers.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
